prompt: Invent a short myth explaining why the sea is salty, in your own style.
task_completions:
Long ago, when the world was still cooling and the mountains were merely pebbles, the Sky and the Sea were deeply in love. The Sky was a creature of shifting moods—sometimes a brilliant, hopeful sapphire, other times a bruised and thundering violet. The Sea was his mirror, a vast, shimmering expanse of silver that spent its days tracing the contours of the clouds.

They lived in a state of perpetual longing, for they could never touch. Whenever the Sky reached down in a sudden rain, he vanished into the depths; whenever the Sea leaped upward in a great wave, he fell back into himself.

To bridge the distance, the Sky crafted a gift: a Great Crystal of Memory. It was a diamond the size of a city, carved from the frozen breath of the first stars. It contained every song ever sung, every secret whispered in the wind, and every dream dreamed by the creatures of the earth. He lowered it slowly on a thread of moonlight, intending for the Sea to hold it as a token of their eternal bond.

But as the Crystal touched the surface, the Earth grew jealous. The Earth, who felt ignored by the lovers above and below, reached up with a sudden, jagged tremor. A massive earthquake shook the foundations of the world, and the Crystal of Memory shattered into a trillion microscopic shards.

The shards were too small to be gathered, too fine to be seen. They dissolved instantly into the water, bleeding their ancient, concentrated essence into the currents.

The Sea did not mourn the loss of the diamond; instead, he found that the shards had changed him. He was no longer just silver water; he was now a reservoir of everything that had ever been. The "salt" we taste today is not salt at all, but the crystallized remnants of those ancient memories—the sting of old heartbreaks, the sharpness of lost joys, and the enduring grit of a love that refused to fade.

This is why the sea is salty, and why, when we swim in its depths, we often feel a strange, inexplicable longing for a home we have never known.

In the First Age, the ocean was not salt, but a vast mirror of sweet, shimmering nectar. It was the drink of the stars, and the creatures that swam within it were made of liquid light and silver song.

At the center of this nectar-sea lived Orym, the Weaver of Tides. Orym was a giant of soft coral and sea-glass, tasked with keeping the currents humming in a perfect, melodic loop. He was a creature of absolute order, but he possessed one forbidden longing: he loved the Moon.

Every night, Orym would reach upward, stretching his crystalline arms to touch the pale, glowing disc of the lunar goddess. But the Moon was distant and cold, and she viewed the world below as a chaotic swirl of foam. She ignored his yearning, sailing her silver ship across the velvet sky without a single glance downward.

For a thousand years, Orym waited. He sang songs that could move mountains of sand, and he sculpted the seabed into intricate palaces of pearl to catch her eye. But the Moon remained indifferent.

One night, the grief became a physical weight in Orym’s chest. It was a heavy, crystalline sorrow that he could no longer carry. He realized that his love was a bridge that would never be crossed, and the realization shattered him. 

Orym did not die, for the sea would not let its weaver perish, but he wept. He wept for the silence of the Moon; he wept for the distance between the water and the stars. He cried for a century, his tears not of water, but of pure, concentrated longing. 

Because Orym was a creature of the deep, his tears were heavy and white, like crushed diamonds. They dissolved into the sweet nectar of the ocean, turning the shimmering waters bitter and sharp. The more he grieved, the more the sea changed, absorbing the salt of his heartbreak until the nectar was gone, replaced by the brine we know today.

Eventually, the Moon looked down and saw the ocean had changed. She saw that the silver mirror had turned a deep, aching blue, seasoned by the salt of a broken heart. Moved by the scale of his devotion, she finally reached out, not with a touch, but with a pull.

To this day, the Moon reaches down to pull the tides toward her, a slow, rhythmic dance of longing. And the sea remains salty, a permanent reminder that the deepest waters are those seasoned by love.

Long ago, when the world was still damp and the mountains were merely mounds of clay, the Sky and the Sea were deeply in love. The Sky was a shimmering veil of sapphire, and the Sea was a mirror of crystal, sweet and fresh as a mountain spring.

They spent eons in a slow, rhythmic dance—the tides reaching up to touch the clouds, and the rain falling down to kiss the waves. But the Sky was restless, forever chasing the wind, while the Sea was possessive, wanting to hold the Sky in her depths forever.

One day, the Sky fell in love with the Land. He became enamored with the scent of pine needles, the jagged peaks of the granite cliffs, and the way the forests breathed in emerald sighs. He began to spend all his time hovering over the continents, painting sunsets over the valleys and whispering secrets to the redwoods.

The Sea watched from below, her currents churning with a cold, heavy jealousy. She tried to pull the Sky back down with great storms and towering waterspouts, but the Sky only laughed, drifting higher and higher, further away from her reach.

Heartbroken and consumed by bitterness, the Sea began to weep. She did not cry soft droplets, but great, heavy torrents of grief. Because her love had turned to resentment, her tears were not sweet like the rain; they were sharp, stinging, and brine-heavy.

She wept for a thousand years, pouring her sorrow into her own depths until the crystal waters turned opaque and heavy. She salted her own heart so that she would never again crave the sweetness of the Sky’s affection.

To this day, the Sea remains salty—a vast, liquid monument to a love that turned to longing, and a longing that turned to salt.
